occurrence.window: US-Israel war on Iran launched 2026-02-28; Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz shortly after; six months in as of late August 2026 with no resolution in sight
occurrence.label: US-Israel-Iran war / Strait of Hormuz closure

title: Iran war at six months: the Hormuz-closure chain beyond the oil-price headline
thesis: The US-Israel war on Iran (launched 2026-02-28) triggered Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz — previously ~25% of world seaborne oil and ~20% of global LNG — producing what analysts call the largest, most durable oil-market disruption in memory. Six months on, the war and the oil price are the most heavily covered macro story on earth, but the chain beneath it — Cape-of-Good-Hope tanker rerouting economics, marine war-risk (re)insurance repricing, a Somali-piracy resurgence exploiting stretched naval patrols, and a broader Gulf-security-architecture reshuffle — sits mostly in trade press, not mainstream financial coverage.
why_now: At the six-month mark (per Washington Post/CSIS reporting, 2026-08-27) there is still no off-ramp; war-risk marine insurance premiums for Hormuz/Persian Gulf transits have spiked >1,000% (from ~0.15-0.25% to 7.5-10% of vessel value per voyage) and the Joint War Committee widened its war-risk zones in March 2026 to cover Bahrain, Djibouti, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the Somali/Pakistani coastlines; Somali pirates hijacked three tankers (MT Honour 25, MT Eureka, MT Asana) between April-July 2026 as ships reroute around Africa and naval patrols are stretched thin across two simultaneous shipping crises (Hormuz + the pre-existing Red Sea/Houthi situation).
retail_gap: Mainstream and retail coverage tracks the war itself and the headline oil price; the tanker-rerouting / marine-war-risk-insurance / piracy-security layer beneath it is covered mainly in energy and insurance trade press (OilPrice, Insurance Business, Insurance Journal, TFTC), rarely reaching general financial media or retail portfolios.

unmappedness.rationale: The occurrence is maximally known — a live war and a closed strait have been the dominant headline for six months, the opposite of obscure. What is unmapped is the specific investable chain underneath it: which insurers/reinsurers are capturing the repriced war risk, which tanker owners capture the ton-mile inflation from Cape rerouting, and who supplies the private maritime security now back in demand — none of which shows up in mainstream 'Iran war' coverage.

evidence.claim: The US and Israel launched war against Iran on 2026-02-28; Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to shipping (previously ~25% of world seaborne oil, ~20% of global LNG); six months later there is still no resolution in sight despite repeated claims a deal was near.
evidence.source_name: Washington Post / CSIS "The Iran War at Six Months" reporting

evidence.claim: War-risk marine insurance premiums for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz/Persian Gulf spiked more than 1,000% (from roughly 0.15-0.25% to 7.5-10% of vessel value per voyage); the Joint War Committee widened its listed war-risk zones in March 2026 to include Bahrain, Djibouti, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the Somali/Pakistani coastlines.
evidence.source_name: Insurance Business magazine / Joint War Committee zone-listing coverage

evidence.claim: Somali piracy resurged as ships reroute around Africa to avoid Hormuz: three tanker hijackings (MT Honour 25, MT Eureka, MT Asana) occurred between April-July 2026 with multi-million-dollar ransom demands, as naval patrols are stretched thin by the simultaneous Hormuz and Red Sea/Houthi situations.
evidence.source_name: CNBC / TFTC Somali piracy surge reporting
